claim: Calcium signals in the axon terminals of olfactory receptor neurons (ORNs) do not follow the same adaptive properties as the firing activity measured at the antenna.
source: We show that calcium signals in the axon terminals of olfactory receptor neurons (ORNs) do not follow the same adaptive properties as the firing activity measured at the antenna.
evidence: This is a primary finding stated in the abstract and supported by experimental data comparing firing rates and calcium responses shown in Figures 1-3.

claim: ORNs calcium responses are sustained on long timescales.
source: While ORNs calcium responses are sustained on long timescales, calcium signals in the postsynaptic projection neurons (PNs) adapt within tens of seconds.
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 1B-C and Figure 4, where ORN calcium responses remain constant over 2 minutes of stimulation.

claim: Calcium signals in the postsynaptic projection neurons (PNs) adapt within tens of seconds.
source: While ORNs calcium responses are sustained on long timescales, calcium signals in the postsynaptic projection neurons (PNs) adapt within tens of seconds.
evidence: This is demonstrated by experimental data in Figures 1B-C and Figure 4, showing exponential decay of PN responses with timescales of 3-10 seconds.

claim: The slow component of the postsynaptic response is mediated by a slow presynaptic depression of vesicle release.
source: We propose that this slow component of the postsynaptic response is mediated by a slow presynaptic depression of vesicle release and enables the combinatorial population activity of PNs to adjust to the mean and variance of fluctuating odor stimuli.
evidence: This is supported by Syp-pHTomato measurements of vesicle release shown in Figure 6, which show slow adaptation matching PN calcium dynamics.

claim: The slow presynaptic depression enables the combinatorial population activity of PNs to adjust to the mean and variance of fluctuating odor stimuli.
source: We propose that this slow component of the postsynaptic response is mediated by a slow presynaptic depression of vesicle release and enables the combinatorial population activity of PNs to adjust to the mean and variance of fluctuating odor stimuli.
evidence: This functional interpretation is supported by data in Figures 8-9 showing that PN populations maintain odor representation while adjusting to stimulus statistics.

claim: A brief exposure to the stimulus can be sufficient for an animal to identify the odor.
source: Whereas a brief exposure to the stimulus can be sufficient for an animal to identify the odor (Bhandawat et al., 2010; Rinberg et al., 2006; Szyszka et al., 2012), changes in stimulus intensity or in higher order statistics, such as variance or temporal correlations, can be used to infer stimulus location (Baker et al., 2018; Celani et al., 2014; Murlis et al., 2000; Vergassola et al., 2007).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to previous studies.

claim: Changes in stimulus intensity or in higher order statistics, such as variance or temporal correlations, can be used to infer stimulus location.
source: Whereas a brief exposure to the stimulus can be sufficient for an animal to identify the odor (Bhandawat et al., 2010; Rinberg et al., 2006; Szyszka et al., 2012), changes in stimulus intensity or in higher order statistics, such as variance or temporal correlations, can be used to infer stimulus location (Baker et al., 2018; Celani et al., 2014; Murlis et al., 2000; Vergassola et al., 2007).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to previous studies.

claim: ORNs usually express a single chemosensory receptor out of a large family of genes.
source: Odor stimuli activate olfactory receptor neurons (ORNs) that usually express a single chemosensory receptor out of a large family of genes (Su et al., 2009; Vosshall and Stocker, 2007).
evidence: This is established knowledge in the field, supported by citations.

claim: Each receptor has different affinities to different odorants, such that a given odor will drive a specific activity pattern across the entire population of ORNs.
source: Each receptor has different affinities to different odorants, such that a given odor will drive a specific activity pattern across the entire population of ORNs (de Bruyne et al., 2001).
evidence: This is established knowledge supported by citation.

claim: ORNs expressing the same receptor innervate the same glomerulus of the antennal lobe.
source: ORNs expressing the same receptor innervate the same glomerulus of the antennal lobe (AL) (Couto et al., 2005; Fishilevich and Vosshall, 2005), within which they synapse onto mostly uniglomerular projection neurons (PNs, Figure 1a) (Marin et al., 2002; Wong et al., 2002).
evidence: This is established anatomical knowledge supported by citations and illustrated in Figure 1a.

claim: ORNs synapse onto mostly uniglomerular projection neurons (PNs) within the antennal lobe.
source: ORNs expressing the same receptor innervate the same glomerulus of the antennal lobe (AL) (Couto et al., 2005; Fishilevich and Vosshall, 2005), within which they synapse onto mostly uniglomerular projection neurons (PNs, Figure 1a) (Marin et al., 2002; Wong et al., 2002).
evidence: This is established anatomical knowledge supported by citations and illustrated in Figure 1a.

claim: Odor stimuli induce specific patterns of activity across glomeruli in the antennal lobe.
source: In the AL, odor stimuli induce specific patterns of activity across glomeruli (Fiala et al., 2002; Wang et al., 2003).
evidence: This is established knowledge supported by citations.

claim: PN responses are shaped by properties of ORN-to-PN synapses, such as short-term presynaptic depression.
source: The PN responses are shaped by properties of ORN-to-PN synapses, such as short-term presynaptic depression (Kazama and Wilson, 2008) and postsynaptic receptor dynamics (Nagel et al., 2015).
evidence: This is established knowledge supported by citations.

claim: PN responses are shaped by postsynaptic receptor dynamics.
source: The PN responses are shaped by properties of ORN-to-PN synapses, such as short-term presynaptic depression (Kazama and Wilson, 2008) and postsynaptic receptor dynamics (Nagel et al., 2015).
evidence: This is established knowledge supported by citations.

claim: A network of local interneurons (LNs) reorganizes the responses of the glomeruli based on the overall activity of the AL by means of both excitatory and inhibitory lateral connection.
source: Moreover, a network of local interneurons (LNs) reorganizes the responses of the glomeruli based on the overall activity of the AL by means of both excitatory (Olsen et al., 2007; Yaksi and Wilson, 2010) and inhibitory lateral connection (Olsen and Wilson, 2008; Root et al., 2008; Silbering and Galizia, 2007).
evidence: This is established knowledge supported by citations.

claim: ORN firing rates adapt to sustained odor stimuli on timescales on the order of ~100 ms.
source: In Drosophila, ORN firing rates adapt to sustained odor stimuli on timescales on the order of ~100 ms (Gorur-Shandilya et al., 2017; Martelli et al., 2013).
evidence: This is established knowledge supported by citations.

claim: ORN firing rate adaptation shifts the dynamic range of the ORN response to match the mean and variance of the stimulus.
source: This adaptation shifts the dynamic range of the ORN response to match the mean and variance of the stimulus (Cafaro, 2016; Gorur-Shandilya et al., 2017).
evidence: This is established knowledge supported by citations.

claim: Previous studies in locusts have reported complex and diverse response dynamics in second-order olfactory neurons.
source: Previous studies in locusts (Geffen et al., 2009; Stopfer et al., 2003), moths (Jacob et al., 2017) and rats (Gupta et al., 2015) have reported complex and diverse response dynamics in second-order olfactory neurons.
evidence: This is established knowledge supported by citations.

claim: Previous studies in moths have reported complex and diverse response dynamics in second-order olfactory neurons.
source: Previous studies in locusts (Geffen et al., 2009; Stopfer et al., 2003), moths (Jacob et al., 2017) and rats (Gupta et al., 2015) have reported complex and diverse response dynamics in second-order olfactory neurons.
evidence: This is established knowledge supported by citations.

claim: Previous studies in rats have reported complex and diverse response dynamics in second-order olfactory neurons.
source: Previous studies in locusts (Geffen et al., 2009; Stopfer et al., 2003), moths (Jacob et al., 2017) and rats (Gupta et al., 2015) have reported complex and diverse response dynamics in second-order olfactory neurons.
evidence: This is established knowledge supported by citations.

claim: Short-term depression, different receptor currents, and lateral inhibition have been identified as mechanisms underlying complex PN response dynamics.
source: In Drosophila, short-term depression, different receptor currents, and lateral inhibition have been identified as mechanisms underlying complex PN response dynamics (Nagel et al., 2015).
evidence: This is established knowledge supported by citation.

claim: Calcium dynamics in ORNs reported by the cytosolic calcium sensor GCaMP3 are similar to the dynamics of the presynaptically targeted calcium sensor Syp-GCaMP3.
source: Calcium dynamics in ORNs reported by the cytosolic calcium sensor CGaMP3 are similar to the dynamics of the presynaptically targeted calcium sensor Syp-GCaMP3 (Pech et al., 2015) (Figure 1D–E) and considerably different from the calcium signals measured from synaptic boutons of PNs in the calyx of the mushroom body (Figure 1D–E).
evidence: This is demonstrated by experimental data shown in Figure 1D-E comparing the two sensors.

claim: Calcium dynamics in ORNs are considerably different from the calcium signals measured from synaptic boutons of PNs in the calyx of the mushroom body.
source: Calcium dynamics in ORNs reported by the cytosolic calcium sensor CGaMP3 are similar to the dynamics of the presynaptically targeted calcium sensor Syp-GCaMP3 (Pech et al., 2015) (Figure 1D–E) and considerably different from the calcium signals measured from synaptic boutons of PNs in the calyx of the mushroom body (Figure 1D–E).
evidence: This is demonstrated by experimental data shown in Figure 1D-E.

claim: The calcium dynamics characterized in ORNs terminals reflect cell-specific synaptic activity.
source: These results indicate that the calcium dynamics characterized in ORNs terminals reflect cell-specific synaptic activity.
evidence: This is an inference based on the comparison of cytosolic and synaptic calcium sensors shown in Figure 1D-E.

claim: The linear filter describes how the response depends on current and past stimuli in a system that is not an instantaneous translator of the stimulus into a response but has a 'memory' for previous stimulations.
source: The linear filter describes how the response depends on current and past stimuli in a system that is not an instantaneous translator of the stimulus into a response but has a 'memory' for previous stimulations.
evidence: This is a general description of linear filter analysis based on established methods.

claim: Different linear filters predict the calcium transients elicited by the random stimulus in ORNs and PNs of the glomerulus DM1.
source: For example, different linear filters predict the calcium transients elicited by the random stimulus in ORNs and PNs of the glomerulus DM1 (Figure 2A and Figure 7—figure supplement 1).
evidence: This is demonstrated by experimental data and analysis shown in Figure 2A and Figure 7—figure supplement 1.

claim: In ORNs, the linear filter is monophasic and can be accurately described by a single exponential function.
source: In ORNs, the linear filter is monophasic and can be accurately described by a single exponential function.
evidence: This is demonstrated by experimental data and modeling shown in Figure 2A.

claim: In PNs, the filter is biphasic with a lagging negative component that indicates adaptation.
source: In PNs, the filter is biphasic with a lagging negative component that indicates adaptation, in the sense that stimuli in the past suppress calcium signals in response to present stimuli.
evidence: This is demonstrated by experimental data and modeling shown in Figure 2A.

claim: Stimuli in the past suppress calcium signals in response to present stimuli in PNs.
source: In PNs, the filter is biphasic with a lagging negative component that indicates adaptation, in the sense that stimuli in the past suppress calcium signals in response to present stimuli.
evidence: This is an interpretation of the biphasic filter shape observed in PNs.

claim: When using the faster fluorescence sensor GCaMP6f, the reverse correlation analysis results in a monophasic filter with a faster timescale (~100 ms).
source: For example, when using the faster fluorescence sensor GCaMP6f, the reverse correlation analysis results also in a monophasic filter, but with a faster timescale (~100 ms, Figure 2B).
evidence: This is demonstrated by experimental data shown in Figure 2B.

claim: The real presynaptic calcium dynamics are likely faster than the sensor kinetics.
source: This suggests that the real presynaptic calcium dynamics are likely faster than the sensor kinetics.
evidence: This is an inference based on the comparison of GCaMP3 and GCaMP6f data.

claim: The deconvolved signal shows fast transients, in accordance with the phasic firing rates of these neurons.
source: The deconvolved signal shows fast transients, in accordance with the phasic firing rates of these neurons.
evidence: This is demonstrated by the deconvolution analysis shown in Figure 2C.

claim: The deconvolution does not affect the response on longer timescales, which remains sustained for the duration of the 2 min stimulation.
source: The deconvolution does not affect the response on longer timescales, which remains sustained for the duration of the 2 min stimulation.
evidence: This is demonstrated by the deconvolution analysis shown in Figure 2C.

claim: Cell- as well as stimulus-specific differences reported by a given sensor are preserved through the deconvolution of the sensor kinetics.
source: Importantly, we assume the same model for the sensor kinetics in different neuron types. This implies that cell- as well as stimulus-specific differences reported by a given sensor are preserved through the deconvolution of the sensor kinetics (see below).
evidence: This is a methodological assumption and inference about the deconvolution approach.

claim: Odor-evoked responses to higher stimulus concentrations can be fitted with similar monophasic linear filters.
source: Odor-evoked responses to higher stimulus concentrations can be fitted with similar monophasic linear filters (Figure 2E).
evidence: This is demonstrated by experimental data and modeling shown in Figure 2E.

claim: Linear filters extracted after deconvolution of the sensor kinetics are faster and with a small negative lobe but are consistently similar at all concentrations.
source: Linear filters can also be extracted after deconvolution of the sensor kinetics. In this case, they are faster and with a small negative lobe (Figure 2I) but are consistently similar at all concentrations.
evidence: This is demonstrated by experimental data and analysis shown in Figure 2I.

claim: The slope of the static function decreases with higher stimulus concentrations, indicating a decreased response gain.
source: Interestingly, the slope of the static function decreases with higher stimulus concentrations (note log scale in the x-axis), indicating a decreased response gain.
evidence: This is demonstrated by experimental data and modeling shown in Figure 2F.

claim: The response to stimuli that shut to zero (plume-like or binary stimuli) are affected by the receptor non-linearity.
source: It has been shown before that the response to stimuli that shut to zero (plume-like or binary stimuli) are indeed affected by the receptor non-linearity (Gorur-Shandilya et al., 2017).
evidence: This is established knowledge supported by citation.

claim: The neuron firing rate in response to isolated odor pulses does not grow linearly with stimulus concentration, but rather shows a sigmoidal dose response curve.
source: This is due to the fact that the neuron firing rate in response to isolated odor pulses does not grow linearly with stimulus concentration, but rather shows a sigmoidal dose response curve (de Bruyne et al., 2001).
evidence: This is established knowledge supported by citation.

claim: When using a front-end non-linearity in the NLN model, the static functions overlap onto a similar shape.
source: When using this non-linearity in front of the LN model (see Materials and methods, NLN model), the static functions overlap onto a similar shape (Figure 2H), also when using the sensor-deconvolved calcium response (Figure 2J).
evidence: This is demonstrated by experimental data and modeling shown in Figure 2H and 2J.

claim: The response gain shows only a small dependency on stimulus mean.
source: The response gain shows only a small dependency on stimulus mean (Figure 2J, inset), demonstrating that a single model of the calcium signals is sufficient to describe the neurons' responses at all stimulus intensities.
evidence: This is demonstrated by experimental data and modeling shown in Figure 2J inset.

claim: A single model of the calcium signals is sufficient to describe the neurons' responses at all stimulus intensities.
source: The response gain shows only a small dependency on stimulus mean (Figure 2J, inset), demonstrating that a single model of the calcium signals is sufficient to describe the neurons' responses at all stimulus intensities.
evidence: This is an inference based on the modeling results shown in Figure 2J.

claim: Apart from a fast transient in the response, little stimulus-driven adaptation occurs in the pre-synaptic calcium at the ORN axon terminals in response to binary stimuli when front-end non-linearities are taken in account.
source: These results suggest that, apart from a fast transient in the response, little stimulus-driven adaptation occurs in the pre-synaptic calcium at the ORN axon terminals in response to binary stimuli when front-end non-linearities are taken in account.
evidence: This is an inference based on the modeling results shown in Figure 2.

claim: The response sensitivity of ORNs decreases when they have adapted to an odor background.
source: It has been previously shown that the response sensitivity of ORNs decreases when they have adapted to an odor background (Martelli et al., 2013) and that the ORN firing rate follows the Weber-Fechner law (Cafaro, 2016; Gorur-Shandilya et al., 2017).
evidence: This is established knowledge supported by citations.

claim: The ORN firing rate follows the Weber-Fechner law.
source: It has been previously shown that the response sensitivity of ORNs decreases when they have adapted to an odor background (Martelli et al., 2013) and that the ORN firing rate follows the Weber-Fechner law (Cafaro, 2016; Gorur-Shandilya et al., 2017).
evidence: This is established knowledge supported by citations.

claim: The firing rate elicited by a pulse of methyl acetate is lower when the pulse is presented on a background of the same odor.
source: Single sensillum recordings (SSR) from ab2A show that the firing rate elicited by a pulse of methyl acetate is lower when the pulse is presented on a background of the same odor (Figure 3B,D,E).
evidence: This is demonstrated by experimental data shown in Figure 3B, D, and E.

claim: The calcium response from the axon terminals of ab2A ORNs is not decreased by an adapting background; rather it is slightly increased.
source: On the contrary, the calcium response from the axon terminals of the same ORN type (innervating DM4) is not decreased by an adapting background; rather it is slightly increased (Figure 3C,D,E).
evidence: This is demonstrated by experimental data shown in Figure 3C, D, and E.

claim: The model predicts a decrease in activity during background presentation and a lower response to the odor pulse when firing rate is convolved with a linear filter modeling the kinetics of the sensors.
source: For both GCaMP3 and GCaMP6f, the model predicts a decrease in activity during background presentation and a lower response to the odor pulse.
evidence: This is demonstrated by modeling shown in Figure 3F.

claim: The actual calcium response is sustained on long timescales and remains always approximately constant (or slightly higher) in response to a pulse independent of background concentration.
source: Rather, the actual calcium response is sustained on long timescales and remains always approximately constant (or slightly higher) in response to a pulse independent of background concentration (Figure 3G).
evidence: This is demonstrated by experimental data shown in Figure 3G.

claim: When the test pulse is lower than the background, the calcium response becomes lower than in the non-adapted condition.
source: However, this is not the case when the test pulse is lower than the background: in this case the calcium response becomes lower than in the non-adapted condition (Figure 3G, orange).
evidence: This is demonstrated by experimental data shown in Figure 3G (orange trace).

claim: The same stimuli elicit a similar range of responses in firing rate and presynaptic calcium.
source: We found that the same stimuli elicit a similar range of responses in firing rate and presynaptic calcium.
evidence: This is demonstrated by experimental data shown in Figure 3H.

claim: Firing rate adaptation occurs for all tested pulse concentrations, even for those close to saturation.
source: Firing rate adaptation occurs for all tested pulse concentrations, even for those close to saturation (Figure 3I, top).
evidence: This is demonstrated by experimental data shown in Figure 3I (top).

claim: Glomerular calcium responses do not decrease upon adaptation, unless the adapting background is higher than the test pulse.
source: On the contrary, glomerular calcium responses do not decrease upon adaptation, unless the adapting background is higher than the test pulse (Figure 3I, bottom).
evidence: This is demonstrated by experimental data shown in Figure 3I (bottom).

claim: Glomerular calcium responses encode increases and decreases in concentration differently.
source: We conclude that glomerular calcium responses do not reflect adaptation observed in firing rate and encode increases and decreases in concentration differently.
evidence: This is an inference based on the experimental data shown in Figure 3.

claim: It took approximately 20 s until the calcium dynamics in PNs reached a steady state.
source: It reproducibly took approximately 20 s until the calcium dynamics reached a steady state.
evidence: This is demonstrated by experimental data shown in Figure 1B and Figure 4.

claim: A slow change in the electrophysiological activity of PNs has been observed upon the onset of a flickering stimulus in flies.
source: A slow change in the electrophysiological activity of PNs has been observed upon the onset of a flickering stimulus in flies (Nagel et al., 2015) and moths (Jacob et al., 2017).
evidence: This is established knowledge supported by citations.

claim: A slow change in the electrophysiological activity of PNs has been observed upon the onset of a flickering stimulus in moths.
source: A slow change in the electrophysiological activity of PNs has been observed upon the onset of a flickering stimulus in flies (Nagel et al., 2015) and moths (Jacob et al., 2017).
evidence: This is established knowledge supported by citations.

claim: The PN responses in DM1 decreased to ~50% of the initial response.
source: The PN responses in DM1 decreased to ~50% of the initial response (Figure 4C, purple).
evidence: This is demonstrated by experimental data shown in Figure 4C.

claim: The decay timescales extracted by the exponential fit ranged between 3 and 10 s for DM1 and showed no dependency on the initial response.
source: The decay timescales extracted by the exponential fit ranged between 3 and 10 s for DM1 and showed no dependency on the initial response (Figure 4D).
evidence: This is demonstrated by experimental data and analysis shown in Figure 4D.

claim: The activity recovered from this slow adaptation within a minute.
source: The activity recovered from this slow adaptation within a minute (Figure 4—figure supplement 1) and it is therefore of a different nature than what was previously observed in the locust (Stopfer and Laurent, 1999) or in the fly (Das et al., 2011).
evidence: This is demonstrated by experimental data shown in Figure 4—figure supplement 1.

claim: The slow adaptation in PNs is of a different nature than what was previously observed in the locust.
source: The activity recovered from this slow adaptation within a minute (Figure 4—figure supplement 1) and it is therefore of a different nature than what was previously observed in the locust (Stopfer and Laurent, 1999) or in the fly (Das et al., 2011).
evidence: This is an inference based on the recovery time shown in Figure 4—figure supplement 1 and comparison with cited studies.

claim: The slow adaptation in PNs is of a different nature than what was previously observed in the fly.
source: The activity recovered from this slow adaptation within a minute (Figure 4—figure supplement 1) and it is therefore of a different nature than what was previously observed in the locust (Stopfer and Laurent, 1999) or in the fly (Das et al., 2011).
evidence: This is an inference based on the recovery time shown in Figure 4—figure supplement 1 and comparison with cited studies.

claim: ORN responses were sustained for 2 min after stimulus onset, with a mean degree of adaptation across glomeruli close to zero.
source: In all cases, ORN responses were sustained for 2 min after stimulus onset, with a mean degree of adaptation across glomeruli close to zero (Figure 4F).
evidence: This is demonstrated by experimental data shown in Figure 4F.

claim: The PN responses in all glomeruli were adaptive, with a mean degree of adaptation across glomeruli equal to 0.57.
source: By contrast, the PN responses in all glomeruli were adaptive, with a mean degree of adaptation across glomeruli equal to 0.57 (Figure 4F).
evidence: This is demonstrated by experimental data shown in Figure 4F.

claim: The adaptation timescale had no clear relation to the amount of initial activity of the glomerulus.
source: The adaptation timescale had no clear relation to the amount of initial activity of the glomerulus (Figure 4G).
evidence: This is demonstrated by experimental data shown in Figure 4G.

claim: Calcium activity in PNs decreases in all glomeruli proportionally to the initial response on timescales that vary in the range between 1 and 40 s, and is glomerulus and concentration dependent.
source: Overall, we conclude from this analysis that calcium activity in PNs decreases in all glomeruli proportionally to the initial response on timescales that vary in the range between 1 and 40 s, and is glomerulus and concentration dependent.
evidence: This is an inference based on the experimental data shown in Figure 4.

claim: Application of PTX increased ORN responses in two glomeruli.
source: Application of PTX increased ORN responses in two glomeruli (Figure 5A–B), and induced a small but significant change in the response amplitude of PNs (Figure 5D and Figure 5—figure supplement 1).
evidence: This is demonstrated by experimental data shown in Figure 5A-B.

claim: Application of PTX induced a small but significant change in the response amplitude of PNs.
source: Application of PTX increased ORN responses in two glomeruli (Figure 5A–B), and induced a small but significant change in the response amplitude of PNs (Figure 5D and Figure 5—figure supplement 1).
evidence: This is demonstrated by experimental data shown in Figure 5D and Figure 5—figure supplement 1.

claim: The degree and timescale of adaptation were similar before and after PTX application.
source: However, the degree and timescale of adaptation were similar before and after PTX application (Figure 5D).
evidence: This is demonstrated by experimental data shown in Figure 5D.

claim: GABA-A receptor activity does not significantly affect PN dynamics on long timescales and cannot solely account for the slow adaptation observed.
source: We conclude that GABA-A receptor activity does not significantly affect PN dynamics on long timescales and cannot solely account for the slow adaptation observed.
evidence: This is an inference based on the PTX experiments shown in Figure 5A-D.

claim: GABA-B receptors in ORNs mediate presynaptic inhibition in ORN terminals in the AL.
source: It has been shown that GABA-B receptors in ORNs mediate presynaptic inhibition in ORN terminals in the AL (Olsen and Wilson, 2008; Root et al., 2008).
evidence: This is established knowledge supported by citations.

claim: Expression of GABA-B receptor RNAi in ORNs affected the initial response of DM4 PNs but not the degree and timescale of adaptation.
source: This manipulation affected the initial response of DM4 PNs (Figures 5E-F and Figure 5—figure supplement 1), but not the degree and timescale of adaptation (Figure 5F).
evidence: This is demonstrated by experimental data shown in Figures 5E-F and Figure 5—figure supplement 1.

claim: CGP54626 application increased the response of glomerulus VM2 to ethyl butyrate and slightly increased the response of DM4, but did not affect DM1 response to methyl acetate.
source: CGP54626 application increased the response of glomerulus VM2 to ethyl butyrate and slightly increased the response of DM4, but did not affect DM1 response to methyl acetate (Figure 5G), in agreement with the results obtained with the RNAi line.
evidence: This is demonstrated by experimental data shown in Figure 5G.

claim: The response of both DM1 ORNs and PNs remained unchanged after CGP54626 application.
source: Accordingly, the response of both DM1 ORNs and PNs remained unchanged after CGP54626 application.
evidence: This is demonstrated by experimental data shown in Figure 5I.

claim: Even though GABA-B mediate inhibition can affect presynaptic activity, the timescales and degree of the stimulus driven depression are not directly controlled by GABA-B.
source: Therefore, even though GABA-B mediate inhibition can affect presynaptic activity, the timescales and degree of the stimulus driven depression are not directly controlled by GABA-B (Figure 5I).
evidence: This is an inference based on the experimental data shown in Figure 5I.

claim: Treatment with the GABA-B agonist SKF97541 decreased the ORN response in all three glomeruli measured.
source: Treatment with the GABA-B agonist SKF97541 decreased the ORN response in all three glomeruli measured (Figure 5H), demonstrating that also DM1 response can be reduced via GABA-B.
evidence: This is demonstrated by experimental data shown in Figure 5H.

claim: Tonic inhibition of the GABA-B receptors strongly affected the response to a fluctuating stimulus.
source: Interestingly, tonic inhibition of the GABA-B receptors strongly affected the response to a fluctuating stimulus.
evidence: This is demonstrated by experimental data shown in Figure 5J.

claim: In DM1 ORNs, the response to the first odor pulse was lower after application of SKF97541, but it increased over the following odor pulses.
source: In DM1 ORNs, the response to the first odor pulse was lower after application of SKF97541 (Figure 5J, top), similarly to the response to the isolated puff, but it increased over the following odor pulses.
evidence: This is demonstrated by experimental data shown in Figure 5J (top).

claim: In PNs, after SKF97541 application, the response slowly decreased and almost disappeared.
source: In PNs, on the contrary, the response slowly decreased and almost disappeared (Figure 5J, bottom).
evidence: This is demonstrated by experimental data shown in Figure 5J (bottom).

claim: The effect of lateral inhibition is activity dependent and tightly tuned to the stimulus input through complex interactions in the AL network.
source: This suggests that the effect of lateral inhibition is activity dependent and tightly tuned to the stimulus input through complex interactions in the AL network, as also shown in Nagel et al. (2015).
evidence: This is an inference based on the experimental data shown in Figure 5J and supported by citation.

claim: GABA-mediated lateral inhibition does not constitute the main mechanisms of the adaptation in PNs.
source: Since the PNs' slow adaptation was observed also in conditions of reduced lateral input, we conclude that GABA-mediated lateral inhibition does not constitute the main mechanisms of the adaptation.
evidence: This is an inference based on the experimental data shown in Figure 5.

claim: The slow adaptation in PNs was observed at low stimulus concentrations that activated only a single glomerulus.
source: The slow adaptation in PNs was also observed at low stimulus concentrations that activated only a single glomerulus, suggesting that the mechanism could be intrinsic to the single glomeruli and not due to computation across glomeruli.
evidence: This is demonstrated by experimental data shown in Figure 4.

claim: The mechanism of slow adaptation could be intrinsic to the single glomeruli and not due to computation across glomeruli.
source: The slow adaptation in PNs was also observed at low stimulus concentrations that activated only a single glomerulus, suggesting that the mechanism could be intrinsic to the single glomeruli and not due to computation across glomeruli.
evidence: This is an inference based on the observation that adaptation occurs even when only a single glomerulus is activated.

claim: The dynamics of postsynaptic calcium in PNs resembled that measured with the cytosolic calcium reporters.
source: The dynamics of postsynaptic calcium in PNs resembled that measured with the cytosolic calcium reporters (Figure 6A).
evidence: This is demonstrated by experimental data shown in Figure 6A.

claim: Vesicle release from ORNs monitored using Syp-pHTomato showed a slow decrease equivalent to the dynamics of the postsynaptic calcium.
source: Interestingly, we observed that vesicle release from ORNs monitored using Syp-pHTomato showed a slow decrease equivalent to the dynamics of the postsynaptic calcium (Figure 6B).
evidence: This is demonstrated by experimental data shown in Figure 6B.

claim: The LN model accurately predicted the synaptic activity of glomerulus DM1.
source: To properly characterize these dynamics, we fitted a LN model to the steady-state Syp-pHTomato signal (Figure 6D) that accurately predicted the synaptic activity of glomerulus DM1 (Figure 6E).
evidence: This is demonstrated by modeling shown in Figure 6D-E.

claim: In all cases, the linear filter of the Syp-pHTomato signal could be fitted by a double exponential with a positive and negative component.
source: In all cases, the linear filter of the Syp-pHTomato signal could be fitted by a double exponential with a positive (A1 >0) and negative (A2 <0) component (BIC <0, Figure 6D and F and Figure 6—figure supplement 1).
evidence: This is demonstrated by modeling shown in Figure 6D, F and Figure 6—figure supplement 1.

claim: The positive component of the Syp-pHTomato filter had a relatively fast timescale (τ1~300–400 ms), similar to the calcium dynamics reported by GCaMP3.
source: The positive component had a relatively fast timescale (τ1~300–400 ms, Figure 6G), similar to the calcium dynamics reported by GCaMP3 (Figure 2E).
evidence: This is demonstrated by modeling shown in Figure 6G and comparison with Figure 2E.

claim: The negative component of the Syp-pHTomato filter had a much slower timescale (τ2) of the order of ~10 s.
source: The negative component instead had a much slower timescale (τ2) of the order of ~10 s (Figure 6G).
evidence: This is demonstrated by modeling shown in Figure 6G.

claim: The slow timescale of the Syp-pHTomato correlates significantly with the corresponding timescales fitted to the decay in cytosolic calcium in PNs.
source: Indeed, it correlates significantly with the corresponding timescales fitted to the decay in cytosolic calcium in PNs (Figure 6H).
evidence: This is demonstrated by correlation analysis shown in Figure 6H.

claim: Slow depression of vesicle release from ORN terminals drives the slow adaptation observed in odorant-evoked calcium responses at PN postsynapses.
source: This result support a model where slow depression of vesicle release from ORN terminals drives the slow adaptation observed in odorant-evoked calcium responses at PN postsynapses.
evidence: This is an inference based on the correlation between Syp-pHTomato and PN calcium dynamics shown in Figure 6.

claim: ORNs calcium responses from different glomeruli were all sustained and could be fitted by monophasic linear filters both with GCaMP3 and GCaMP6f.
source: ORNs calcium responses from different glomeruli were all sustained and could be fitted by monophasic linear filters both with GCaMP3 (Figure 7A) and GCaMP6f (Figure 1—figure supplement 2A).
evidence: This is demonstrated by experimental data and modeling shown in Figure 7A and Figure 1—figure supplement 2A.

claim: Some glomeruli had faster responses than others (e.g. DC1 and DL5).
source: Some glomeruli had faster responses than others (e.g. DC1 and DL5).
evidence: This is demonstrated by experimental data shown in Figure 7A.

claim: These differences in response speed between glomeruli were robust to deconvolution of the sensor kinetics.
source: These differences were robust to deconvolution of the sensor kinetics (Figure 7B), demonstrating that the calcium dynamics reported by GCaMPs can be used for internal comparisons (between glomeruli or cell types).
evidence: This is demonstrated by analysis shown in Figure 7B.

claim: The calcium dynamics reported by GCaMPs can be used for internal comparisons (between glomeruli or cell types).
source: These differences were robust to deconvolution of the sensor kinetics (Figure 7B), demonstrating that the calcium dynamics reported by GCaMPs can be used for internal comparisons (between glomeruli or cell types).
evidence: This is an inference based on the robustness of differences after deconvolution shown in Figure 7B.

claim: All ORNs filters could be fitted by a single exponential function, apart from a constant which captured non-stationary features of nearly saturated responses.
source: All ORNs filters could be fitted by a single exponential function (Figure 7A), apart from a constant which captured non-stationary features of nearly saturated responses (DL5 and DM4, Figure 7A).
evidence: This is demonstrated by modeling shown in Figure 7A.

claim: The fitted timescales for ORN filters ranged between 300 ms and 1 s.
source: The fitted timescales ranged between 300 ms and 1 s, and we did not observe any consistent dependence of these timescales on response amplitude within single glomeruli (Figure 7C,D).
evidence: This is demonstrated by modeling shown in Figure 7C-D.

claim: There was no consistent dependence of ORN filter timescales on response amplitude within single glomeruli.
source: The fitted timescales ranged between 300 ms and 1 s, and we did not observe any consistent dependence of these timescales on response amplitude within single glomeruli (Figure 7C,D).
evidence: This is demonstrated by modeling shown in Figure 7C-D.

claim: A two-way analysis of variance suggested that the response timescale depended more strongly on glomerulus type (p<10−6) than on concentration.
source: A two-way analysis of variance suggested that the response timescale depended more strongly on glomerulus type (p<10−6) than on concentration.
evidence: This is demonstrated by statistical analysis of the data shown in Figure 7D.

claim: The timescales inferred from calcium responses should be considered as upper bounds of the real timescale since the measured calcium signals are limited by the kinetics of the sensor.
source: The timescales inferred from calcium responses should be considered as upper bounds of the real timescale since the measured calcium signals are limited by the kinetics of the sensor.
evidence: This is an inference based on the known limitations of calcium sensors.

claim: PNs respond faster than ORNs to odor stimuli as a result of short-term synaptic depression.
source: Drosophila PNs respond faster than ORNs to odor stimuli (Bhandawat et al., 2007) as a result of short-term synaptic depression (Kazama and Wilson, 2008).
evidence: This is established knowledge supported by citations.

claim: After the initial adaptation period, odor-elicited calcium responses in PNs could be described by an LN model.
source: As previously shown in second-order olfactory neurons firing activity (Geffen et al., 2009; Gupta et al., 2015; Jacob et al., 2017), after the initial adaptation period, odor-elicited calcium responses could also be described by an LN model (Figure 7E).
evidence: This is demonstrated by modeling shown in Figure 7E and supported by citations.

claim: The linear filter of the PNs is not monophasic, as for the corresponding ORNs, but shows a negative component.
source: The linear filter of the PNs is not monophasic, as for the corresponding ORNs, but shows a negative component (see DM2 in Figure 7A and E).
evidence: This is demonstrated by modeling shown in Figure 7A and E.

claim: The PNs linear filters gradually shifted from biphasic to monophasic as the concentration increased.
source: Importantly, the PNs linear filters gradually shifted from biphasic to monophasic as the concentration increased (e.g. DM1 in Figure 7E).
evidence: This is demonstrated by modeling shown in Figure 7E.

claim: These concentration dependent differences in PN filters were observed also after deconvolution of the sensor kinetics.
source: These concentration dependent differences were observed also after deconvolution of the sensor kinetics (Figure 7F).
evidence: This is demonstrated by analysis shown in Figure 7F.

claim: There was a significant dependence of the model selected on the response amplitude: the filter shape was usually monophasic at very low responses, biphasic at intermediate responses, and then again monophasic at high responses.
source: However, we found a significant dependence of the model selected on the response amplitude: the filter shape was usually monophasic at very low responses, biphasic at intermediate responses, and then again monophasic at high responses (Figure 7—figure supplement 2D, Kruskal-Wallis test, p<0.02).
evidence: This is demonstrated by statistical analysis shown in Figure 7—figure supplement 2D.

claim: At low responses there is little synaptic depression between ORNs and PNs, which becomes stronger at intermediate stimulus intensity, making the PN response more biphasic and differentiating.
source: One possible interpretation of our results is that at low responses there is little synaptic depression between ORNs and PNs, which becomes stronger at intermediate stimulus intensity, making the PN response more biphasic and differentiating.
evidence: This is a speculative interpretation of the concentration-dependent filter shapes.

claim: Stronger responses probably engage additional mechanisms (lateral inputs or postsynaptic modulation) with their own dynamics and also drive the response towards saturation.
source: Stronger responses probably engage additional mechanisms (lateral inputs or postsynaptic modulation) with their own dynamics (Geffen et al., 2009) and also drive the response towards saturation.
evidence: This is a speculative interpretation supported by citation.

claim: Summing feedforward ORN inputs through depressing synapses with stimulus-specific lateral inputs induces strong non-linearities in the PN output dynamics across concentrations.
source: Summing feedforward ORN inputs through depressing synapses with stimulus-specific lateral inputs certainly induce strong non-linearities in the PN output dynamics across concentrations (Figure 7—figure supplement 2A–C), similarly to what found in mitral/tufted cells (Gupta et al., 2015).
evidence: This is an inference based on the data shown in Figure 7—figure supplement 2A-C and supported by citation.

claim: The LN model confirms that PNs calcium responses are more adaptive than ORNs, and the specific dynamics (filter shape) of different glomeruli are concentration dependent.
source: In conclusion, the LN model confirms that PNs calcium responses are more adaptive than ORNs, and the specific dynamics (filter shape) of different glomeruli are concentration dependent.
evidence: This is an inference based on the modeling results shown in Figure 7.

claim: Combinatorial ORN responses were stationary over a time period of 2 min.
source: Combinatorial ORN responses were stationary over a time period of 2 min and, consequently, the population responses to the first odor pulse were very similar to the responses to a pulse 2 min later (Figure 8A).
evidence: This is demonstrated by PCA analysis shown in Figure 8A.

claim: The population responses to the first odor pulse were very similar to the responses to a pulse 2 min later in ORNs.
source: Combinatorial ORN responses were stationary over a time period of 2 min and, consequently, the population responses to the first odor pulse were very similar to the responses to a pulse 2 min later (Figure 8A).
evidence: This is demonstrated by PCA analysis shown in Figure 8A.

claim: The combinatorial representation of the stimulus changed over time in PNs.
source: On the contrary, the combinatorial representation of the stimulus changed over time in PNs (Figure 8B).
evidence: This is demonstrated by PCA analysis shown in Figure 8B.

claim: The calcium signal from single glomeruli decreased proportionally to the peak response.
source: Since the calcium signal from single glomeruli decreased proportionally to the peak response (Figure 4), the combinatorial activity represented by the PC1 scaled linearly and resulted in a multiplicative rescaling of the ORN-to-PN transformation (Figure 8C).
evidence: This is demonstrated by data shown in Figure 4 and analysis shown in Figure 8C.

claim: The combinatorial activity represented by the PC1 scaled linearly and resulted in a multiplicative rescaling of the ORN-to-PN transformation.
source: Since the calcium signal from single glomeruli decreased proportionally to the peak response (Figure 4), the combinatorial activity represented by the PC1 scaled linearly and resulted in a multiplicative rescaling of the ORN-to-PN transformation (Figure 8C).
evidence: This is demonstrated by PCA analysis shown in Figure 8C.

claim: Slow synaptic adaptation adjusts the PN response, while preserving the odor representation at the population level.
source: These results show that slow synaptic adaptation adjusts the PN response, while preserving the odor representation at the population level.
evidence: This is an inference based on the PCA analysis shown in Figure 8.

claim: Increasing the concentration of an odorant led to more active glomeruli by recruiting ORNs that express receptors with lower odorant affinities.
source: Increasing the concentration of an odorant led to more active glomeruli by recruiting ORNs that express receptors with lower odorant affinities (Figure 9A).
evidence: This is demonstrated by experimental data shown in Figure 9A.

claim: As the concentration increased, the response of ORNs in individual glomeruli saturated and their dynamic range shrank.
source: As the concentration increased, the response of ORNs in individual glomeruli saturated and their dynamic range shrank, as shown by the large offset in the static nonlinearity for high concentrations (Figure 9B, top).
evidence: This is demonstrated by experimental data and modeling shown in Figure 9B (top).

claim: Responses of PNs spanned a wider dynamic range than ORNs.
source: However, responses of the corresponding PNs spanned a wider dynamic range (Figure 9B, bottom).
evidence: This is demonstrated by experimental data and modeling shown in Figure 9B (bottom).

claim: In ORNs, the coding of stimulus fluctuations might shift from one subset of glomeruli to another as the odorant concentration changes while being more distributed in the population of PNs.
source: This suggests that, in ORNs, the coding of stimulus fluctuations might shift from one subset of glomeruli to another as the odorant concentration changes while being more distributed in the population of PNs (Figure 8—figure supplement 1).
evidence: This is an inference based on the data shown in Figure 9B and Figure 8—figure supplement 1.

claim: For increasing odorant concentrations in ORNs, the dynamic range of the combinatorial representation shifted along a single dimension.
source: For increasing odorant concentrations in ORNs, the dynamic range of the combinatorial representation shifted along this single dimension (x-axis, Figure 9C), whereas in PNs the dynamic range stretched (y-axis, Figure 9C).
evidence: This is demonstrated by PCA analysis shown in Figure 9C.

claim: In PNs the dynamic range stretched with increasing odorant concentrations.
source: For increasing odorant concentrations in ORNs, the dynamic range of the combinatorial representation shifted along this single dimension (x-axis, Figure 9C), whereas in PNs the dynamic range stretched (y-axis, Figure 9C).
evidence: This is demonstrated by PCA analysis shown in Figure 9C.

claim: The CV of the neural response is expected to be lower because of the neuron integration time (CV = 0.45).
source: The CV of the neural response is expected to be lower because of the neuron integration time (CV = 0.45; see Materials and methods), but still independent of concentration if the coding of stimulus fluctuations was accurate.
evidence: This is a theoretical expectation based on modeling described in Materials and methods.

claim: The CV dropped from 0.45 to 0.15 in ORNs as concentration increased, but stayed fairly constant in PNs.
source: Interestingly, we found that although the CV dropped from 0.45 to 0.15 in ORNs as concentration increased, it stayed fairly constant in PNs (Figure 9D).
evidence: This is demonstrated by experimental data shown in Figure 9D.

claim: Adaptation in the responses of single PN types allows the glomerular PN populations to robustly encode both the mean and the variance of the stimulus over a larger range of concentrations than ORNs.
source: We conclude that adaption in the responses of single PN types allows the glomerular PN populations to robustly encode both the mean and the variance of the stimulus over a larger range of concentrations than ORNs.
evidence: This is an inference based on the experimental data shown in Figure 9.

claim: Presynaptic calcium signals from the primary olfactory sensors, the ORNs, as reported by fluorescent indicators, do not show the same adaptation properties as the firing measured in the dendrites of the same neurons.
source: Our experiments revealed that presynaptic calcium signals from the primary olfactory sensors, the ORNs, as reported by fluorescent indicators, do not show the same adaptation properties as the firing measured in the dendrites of the same neurons.
evidence: This is a summary of the main finding demonstrated throughout the paper, particularly in Figures 1-3.

claim: On short timescales (~100 ms), the true calcium dynamics are certainly affected by the sensor kinetics and a linear deconvolution recapitulates some of the phasic properties of the firing rate.
source: On short timescales (~100 ms), the true calcium dynamics are certainly affected by the sensor kinetics and a linear deconvolution (Figure 2) recapitulates some of the phasic properties of the firing rate.
evidence: This is demonstrated by the deconvolution analysis shown in Figure 2.

claim: A direct comparison between firing rate and calcium response to isolated odor pulses demonstrates a striking correspondence in two neuron types, suggesting a similar working range of the sensor in these two cell types.
source: However, a direct comparison between firing rate and calcium response to isolated odor pulses (Figure 3) demonstrates a striking correspondence in two neuron types, suggesting a similar working range of the sensor in these two cell types.
evidence: This is demonstrated by experimental data shown in Figure 3.

claim: Inhibitory lateral inputs have their own transient dynamics.
source: Inhibitory lateral inputs have their own transient dynamics (Nagel et al., 2015), therefore one possibility could be that inhibition suppresses the initial calcium response stronger than the later response.
evidence: This is established knowledge supported by citation.

claim: Sustained activity in ORNs was observed even at very low concentrations that activate a single glomerulus.
source: However, we observed sustained activity in ORNs even at very low concentrations that activate a single glomerulus and the sustained ORN response could not be altered by blocking GABA receptors.
evidence: This is demonstrated by experimental data shown in Figure 4 and Figure 5.

claim: The sustained ORN response could not be altered by blocking GABA receptors.
source: However, we observed sustained activity in ORNs even at very low concentrations that activate a single glomerulus and the sustained ORN response could not be altered by blocking GABA receptors.
evidence: This is demonstrated by experimental data shown in Figure 5.

claim: Calcium at the ORNs presynapses is regulated in a way to extract certain features of the stimulus from firing activity, either by lateral inputs or cell autonomously.
source: The other possibility is that calcium at the ORNs presynapses is regulated in a way to extract certain features of the stimulus from firing activity, either by lateral inputs or cell autonomously, for example through expression of different voltage-gated calcium channels (Gu et al., 2009; Iniguez et al., 2013), activity-dependent modulation of their expression (Gratz et al., 2018) and function (Dason et al., 2012).
evidence: This is a speculative interpretation supported by citations.

claim: The firing rate follows the Weber-Fechner law and adapts to stimulus mean and variance.
source: While it remains certainly true that the firing rate follows the Weber-Fechner law and adapts to stimulus mean and variance (Gorur-Shandilya et al., 2017), the implications for coding are different depending on whether these properties are transmitted downstream from the antenna or whether they play a different function in calcium regulation at the presynapses.
evidence: This is established knowledge supported by citation.

claim: The PN adaptive capabilities rely mostly on properties of the ORN-PN synapses.
source: Previous studies have suggested that the PN adaptive capabilities rely mostly on properties of the ORN-PN synapses (Cafaro, 2016; Kazama and Wilson, 2008; Nagel et al., 2015).
evidence: This is established knowledge supported by citations.

claim: A combination of slow and fast dynamics occurs at ORN-PN synapses that allows the population of PNs to maintain a neural representation of the stimulus identity and statistics (i.e. mean and variance).
source: Here, we show that a combination of slow and fast dynamics occurs at these synapses that allows the population of PNs to maintain a neural representation of the stimulus identity and statistics (i.e. mean and variance).
evidence: This is a summary of the main finding demonstrated throughout the paper, particularly in Figures 6-9.

claim: On short timescales, PNs calcium responses can be modeled by fast biphasic linear filters that underlie their capability to sense fast changes in concentration.
source: On short timescales, PNs calcium responses can be modeled by fast biphasic linear filters that underlie their capability to sense fast changes in concentration (Bhandawat et al., 2007; Kim et al., 2015).
evidence: This is demonstrated by modeling shown in Figure 7 and supported by citations.

claim: The biphasic response in PNs is consistent with the property and function of previously described short-term presynaptic depression, a mechanisms that enhances neural temporal coding.
source: This biphasic response is consistent with the property and function of previously described short-term presynaptic depression, a mechanisms that enhances neural temporal coding (Tsodyks and Markram, 1997) as reported also in other insects (Huston et al., 2015).
evidence: This is an inference based on the biphasic filter shape and supported by citations.

claim: pH-dependent sensors of synaptic vesicle release have been previously used in both vertebrates and insects.
source: pH-dependent sensors of synaptic vesicle release have been previously used in both vertebrates (Dreosti et al., 2009; Miesenböck et al., 1998) and insects (Ng et al., 2002; Pech et al., 2015; Yu et al., 2004).
evidence: This is established knowledge supported by citations.

claim: pH-dependent sensors made it possible to characterize synaptic depression and facilitation that mediate adaptation in the visual system.
source: In particular, they made it possible to characterize synaptic depression and facilitation that mediate adaptation in the visual system (Nikolaev et al., 2013).
evidence: This is established knowledge supported by citation.

claim: Short-term plasticity results mostly from an interplay between calcium-dependent modulation of the probability of vesicle release and the depletion of available vesicles.
source: These forms of short-term plasticity result mostly from an interplay between calcium-dependent modulation of the probability of vesicle release and the depletion of available vesicles.
evidence: This is established knowledge in the field.

claim: The simplest model of synaptic depression consists of a finite pool of ready-releasable vesicles that is replenished from an infinite pool at a certain limiting rate.
source: The simplest model of synaptic depression consists of a finite pool of ready-releasable vesicles that is replenished from an infinite pool at a certain limiting rate (Abbott, 1997).
evidence: This is established knowledge supported by citation.

claim: Synaptic depression at the neuromuscular junctions of Drosophila larva can be described by a model in which the supply pool is finite and is itself replenished at slower time-scales (~10 s) by a larger reservoir.
source: Synaptic depression at the neuromuscular junctions of Drosophila larva can be described by a model in which the supply pool is finite and is itself replenished at slower time-scales (~10 s) by a larger reservoir (Hallermann et al., 2010).
evidence: This is established knowledge supported by citation.

claim: Our current understanding of ORN-to-PN synapses is insufficient to point to a specific model of synaptic depression.
source: However, other models are also possible and our current understanding of ORN-to-PN synapses is insufficient to point to a specific one.
evidence: This is an acknowledgment of the limitations of current knowledge.

claim: In presence of a sustained stimulus that activates multiple glomeruli, tonic activation of the GABA-ergic pathway does not simply decrease presynaptic activity releasing depression, rather it disrupts the entraining of the network with the stimulus, resulting in a loss of temporal resolution and response in PNs.
source: However, in presence of a sustained stimulus that activates multiple glomeruli, tonic activation of the GABA-ergic pathway does not simply decrease presynaptic activity releasing depression, as one would expect, rather it disrupts the entraining of the network with the stimulus, resulting in a loss of temporal resolution and response in PNs (Figure 5J).
evidence: This is demonstrated by experimental data shown in Figure 5J.

claim: Under sustained stimulation, changes in the activity of LNs as well as recurrent connections within the AL could affect the coupling between inhibition and depression at the ORN presynapses.
source: It is likely that under sustained stimulation, changes in the activity of LNs (Nagel et al., 2015) as well as recurrent connections within the AL could affect the coupling between inhibition and depression at the ORN presynapses.
evidence: This is a speculative interpretation supported by citation.

claim: It remains unclear whether the slow adaptation described here can be solely explained by presynaptic mechanisms or whether involves post-synaptic dynamics as well.
source: Finally, it remains unclear whether the slow adaptation described here can be solely explained by presynaptic mechanisms or whether involves post-synaptic dynamics as well (Cafaro, 2016; Nagel et al., 2015).
evidence: This is an acknowledgment of uncertainty supported by citations.

claim: Retinal ganglion cells adapt their sensitivity to a change in the visual stimulus on both short (<100 ms) and slow timescales (~10 s).
source: For example, retinal ganglion cells adapt their sensitivity to a change in the visual stimulus on both short (<100 ms) and slow timescales (~10 s) (Chander and Chichilnisky, 2001).
evidence: This is established knowledge supported by citation.

claim: Auditory neurons in songbirds slowly adapt their firing to stimulus variance, but instantaneously adapt their filter shape and gain.
source: Similarly, auditory neurons in songbirds slowly adapt their firing to stimulus variance, but instantaneously adapt their filter shape and gain (Nagel and Doupe, 2006).
evidence: This is established knowledge supported by citation.

claim: Fast adaptation acts as a gain control mechanism that prevents saturation by decreasing sensitivity, while slow adaptation allows adjustment to the overall variance of the stimulus.
source: These two forms of adaptation play different roles in sensory coding. Fast adaptation acts as a gain control mechanism that prevents saturation by decreasing sensitivity, while slow adaptation allows adjustment to the overall variance of the stimulus (Baccus and Meister, 2002).
evidence: This is established knowledge supported by citation.

claim: Adaptation can occur on a continuum of timescales, from milliseconds to minutes and involve several mechanisms.
source: Adaptation can, in principle, occur on a continuum of timescales, from milliseconds to minutes (Fairhall et al., 2001) and involve several mechanisms.
evidence: This is established knowledge supported by citation.

claim: Potassium conductance mediates slow contrast adaptation in visual cortical neurons by a purely cellular mechanism.
source: For example, potassium conductance mediates slow contrast adaptation in visual cortical neurons by a purely cellular mechanism (Sanchez-Vives et al., 2000).
evidence: This is established knowledge supported by citation.

claim: Network mechanisms can explain slow adaptation in ganglion cells as a result of reduced presynaptic glutamate release.
source: Network mechanisms can explain slow adaptation in ganglion cells as a result of reduced presynaptic glutamate release (Manookin and Demb, 2006).
evidence: This is established knowledge supported by citation.

claim: Both depression and facilitation mediate adaptation to contrast in the zebrafish retina.
source: Both depression and facilitation mediate adaptation to contrast in the zebrafish retina (Nikolaev et al., 2013).
evidence: This is established knowledge supported by citation.

claim: Not only fast, but also slow adaptation in the olfactory PNs of Drosophila can be attributed to depression of presynaptic activity.
source: Here, we report that not only fast, but also slow adaptation in the olfactory PNs of Drosophila can be attributed to depression of presynaptic activity.
evidence: This is a summary of the main finding demonstrated throughout the paper, particularly in Figure 6.

claim: Our data, together with previously reported fast and slow postsynaptic currents, support a major role of the synapse in adaptive coding.
source: Our data, together with previously reported fast and slow postsynaptic currents (Nagel et al., 2015), support a major role of the synapse in adaptive coding.
evidence: This is an inference based on the current data and supported by citation.

claim: These findings do not exclude that additional network or cellular mechanisms are involved in adaptation on different timescales or under different stimulus conditions.
source: These findings do not exclude that additional network or cellular mechanisms are involved in adaptation on different timescales or under different stimulus conditions.
evidence: This is an acknowledgment of the limitations of the current findings.

claim: Divisive normalization has been identified as a neural computation implemented in the antennal lobe by a network of inhibitory local interneurons.
source: Previous studies have identified divisive normalization as a neural computation implemented in the antennal lobe by a network of inhibitory local interneurons (Olsen et al., 2010), which scales the response of single neurons by the overall population activity (Carandini and Heeger, 2011).
evidence: This is established knowledge supported by citations.

claim: Divisive normalization scales the response of single neurons by the overall population activity.
source: Previous studies have identified divisive normalization as a neural computation implemented in the antennal lobe by a network of inhibitory local interneurons (Olsen et al., 2010), which scales the response of single neurons by the overall population activity (Carandini and Heeger, 2011).
evidence: This is established knowledge supported by citations.

claim: In the olfactory system, divisive normalization is believed to enhance the dynamic range of PNs.
source: It can serve a diversity of functions, but in the olfactory system it is believed to enhance the dynamic range of PNs (Galizia, 2014; Wang, 2012).
evidence: This is established knowledge supported by citations.

claim: GABA and the expression of GABA-B receptors in ORNs mediate lateral inhibition by modulating calcium responses in ORN terminals.
source: Root et al. (2008) have shown that GABA and the expression of GABA-B receptors in ORNs mediate this lateral inhibition by modulating calcium responses in ORN terminals.
evidence: This is established knowledge supported by citation.

claim: Presynaptic lateral inhibition should not be the main determinant of the ORN-to-PN transformation described here, although it affects presynaptic activity.
source: Therefore, presynaptic lateral inhibition should not be the main determinant of the ORN-to-PN transformation described here, although it of course affects presynaptic activity.
evidence: This is an inference based on the experimental data shown in Figure 5.

claim: Divisive normalization and slow depression are two complementary mechanisms that adjust the PNs dynamic range.
source: We conclude that divisive normalization and slow depression are two complementary mechanisms that adjust the PNs dynamic range.
evidence: This is an inference based on the experimental data and comparison with previous studies.

claim: While the lateral inhibition scales responses based on overall network activity, the slow depression adjusts the response gain to the statistics (mean and variance) of the incoming stimuli.
source: While the lateral inhibition scales responses based on overall network activity (Olsen et al., 2010), the slow depression described here adjusts the response gain to the statistics (mean and variance) of the incoming stimuli.
evidence: This is an inference based on the experimental data shown in Figures 6-9 and comparison with cited studies.

claim: Lateral inhibition depends on the connectivity of the AL network and affects different glomeruli differently.
source: Moreover, lateral inhibition depends on the connectivity of the AL network and, therefore, affects different glomeruli differently.
evidence: This is established knowledge in the field.

claim: The slow adaptation depends on feed-forward connectivity and proportionally scales combinatorial odor presentations.
source: On the contrary, the slow adaptation depends on feed-forward connectivity and proportionally scales combinatorial odor presentations.
evidence: This is an inference based on the experimental data shown in Figure 8.

claim: Flies respond with an increase in upwind velocity to odor onset which adapts on a timescale of ~10 s.
source: A recent work on odor driven walking behavior has shown that flies respond with an increase in upwind velocity to odor onset which adapts on a timescale of ~10 s (Álvarez-Salvado et al., 2018).
evidence: This is established knowledge supported by citation.

claim: The adaptation timescale of ~10 s in walking behavior cannot be explained with ORN firing rate adaptation (that is much faster ~100 ms), but it is in agreement with the slow presynaptic depression identified here.
source: This adaptation timescale cannot be explained with ORN firing rate adaptation (that is much faster ~100 ms), but it is surprisingly in agreement with the slow presynaptic depression identified here.
evidence: This is an inference connecting the current findings with behavioral data from a cited study.

claim: Animals that use olfaction to localize a source will likely implement different strategies depending on the statistics of the odor landscape.
source: Animals that use olfaction to localize a source will likely implement different strategies depending on the statistics of the odor landscape (Baker et al., 2018; Gaudry et al., 2012) and the availability of different timescales for the sensory processing of the stimulus may allow them to flexibly adapt their search strategy.
evidence: This is a speculative interpretation supported by citations.

claim: The availability of different timescales for the sensory processing of the stimulus may allow animals to flexibly adapt their search strategy.
source: Animals that use olfaction to localize a source will likely implement different strategies depending on the statistics of the odor landscape (Baker et al., 2018; Gaudry et al., 2012) and the availability of different timescales for the sensory processing of the stimulus may allow them to flexibly adapt their search strategy.
evidence: This is a speculative interpretation of the functional implications of the findings.

claim: A linear combination of glomeruli activity represents the stimulus identity during a highly dynamic stimulation and this combination scales proportionally for different mean values of this stimulus.
source: Here, we have demonstrated that a linear combination of glomeruli activity represents the stimulus identity during a highly dynamic stimulation and this combination scales proportionally for different mean values of this stimulus.
evidence: This is demonstrated by PCA analysis shown in Figure 8.

claim: This combinatorial representation is stationary over time in ORNs, but undergoes a slow rearrangement in the space of PNs.
source: This combinatorial representation is stationary over time in ORNs, but undergoes a slow rearrangement in the space of PNs.
evidence: This is demonstrated by PCA analysis shown in Figure 8.

claim: The rearrangement in PN space consists of a linear scaling of population activity that preserves information about both stimulus identity (same population of neurons) and intensity (same order of stimuli).
source: This rearrangement consists of a linear scaling of population activity that preserves information about both stimulus identity (same population of neurons) and intensity (same order of stimuli).
evidence: This is demonstrated by PCA analysis shown in Figure 8.

claim: Animals that navigate a turbulent odor landscape will experience increased stimulus variance and increased stimulus intensity as they approach the odor source.
source: Animals that navigate a turbulent odor landscape will experience increased stimulus variance and increased stimulus intensity as they approach the odor source (Celani et al., 2014).
evidence: This is established knowledge supported by citation.

claim: The mechanisms described here can explain how odor perception is preserved while the animal moves toward an odor source and the sensory system dynamically adjusts its activity to better represent the statistical context of the odor signal.
source: The mechanisms described here can explain how odor perception is preserved while the animal moves toward an odor source and the sensory system dynamically adjusts its activity to better represent the statistical context of the odor signal.
evidence: This is a speculative interpretation of the functional implications of the findings.
